as_of.observation_horizon: year-to-date with emphasis on the first half

input.raw_text: The dollar is having its worst stretch in years — the index is down around ten percent since January, the worst first half I can remember in decades — and the usual playbook of hiding in US mega-caps while the currency does the work is simply not paying. For the first time in a long while, international equities are beating the S&P: European banks and defense names have ripped, the DAX is out front, and even Japanese stocks in dollar terms are keeping pace. I keep hearing it dismissed as a weak-dollar trade, but flows tell another story — global funds that have underweighted the rest of the world for a decade are quietly rebuilding non-US positions. Call it dollar weakness, call it valuation relief; either way, the crowd is on the wrong side of it.
input.summary: The commentary describes a roughly ten percent year-to-date decline in the dollar index alongside international equity outperformance versus the S&P 500. European banks, European defense companies, the DAX, and Japanese equities in dollar terms are identified as notable areas of strength. The relative performance is attributed not only to dollar weakness and valuation relief but also to global funds rebuilding non-US equity exposure after a prolonged period of underweighting, though the durability and precise cause of the shift remain uncertain.
